extracted.intended_audience: regulated employers, industry stakeholders, economists, and public commenters on OSHA's heat standard NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodology OSHA uses to evaluate the economic feasibility and cost impacts of the proposed heat-protection standard, including screening tests, data sources, time parameters, sensitivity analyses, and factors bearing on ability to absorb or pass on costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue screening test (1% of annual revenues)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA generally considers a standard to be economically feasible for an affected industry when the annualized costs of compliance are less than one percent of annual revenues for the average establishment in an industry that incurs an obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-percent revenue threshold is intentionally set at a low level so OSHA can confidently assert feasibility for industries below the threshold. The revenue test measures annualized costs against annual revenues for establishments that will incur obligations under the proposed standard (not against all establishments in the industry). Industries failing this screen are flagged for further examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuation of profit screening test
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA has discontinued use of the prior profit-screen (e.g., costs as a percent of annual profits) for the proposed standard and will rely on the revenue test instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given include: OSHA is virtually alone in using a profitability test; profit data are unreliable, lack transparency, and have incomplete coverage; firms may manipulate reported profits for tax purposes; available IRS profit data are aggregated and incompatible with the needed NAICS detail; profit screens can produce misleading flags (e.g., nonprofits, industries with missing data). OSHA notes EPA and other agencies rely on sales/revenue tests. OSHA will still examine industries that fail the revenue screen via further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of denominator for cost-to-revenue ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When OSHA speaks of costs as a percent of revenues, it refers to the costs of complying with the standard for the subset of establishments that will incur obligations under the proposed standard, not to all establishments in an industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach avoids underestimating average per-establishment cost used in the feasibility analysis, even if it may overstate the impact on the industry as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time parameters for analysis (annual basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's economic analyses almost always measure the costs of a standard on an annual basis, conducting the screening tests by measuring the cost of the standard against the annual revenues for a given industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One year is typically the minimum period for evaluating business status. Although some compliance costs are up-front and some spread over time, OSHA bases feasibility analysis on annual costs and revenues for this permanent standard. This is consistent with OSHA's typical methodology (e.g., final Silica rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensitivity analyses to test robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA presents results of multiple sensitivity analyses in which isolated changes are made to cost model input parameters to illustrate how adjustments impact estimated total costs of the proposed standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the cost model methodology and calculations are generally linear and additive, sensitivity of results will generally be proportional to isolated parameter changes. OSHA conducted five sensitivity tests (detailed below) and invites public input on assumptions, data, and methodological approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity test — percentage of buildings considered adequately cooled
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary assumption: considered all buildings with at least 51 percent of floorspace cooled as adequately cooled. Sensitivity assumption: considered buildings with 70 percent of floorspace cooled as adequately cooled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used CBECS data and a specific method (60 percent of the percentage of buildings with 51–99% floorspace cooled plus percentage with 100% cooled) to estimate adequately cooled establishments. Changing the cooled-percent threshold increased estimated annualized costs by $585 million (about 7.5%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity test — rest break non-compliance rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary assumption: rest break non-compliance rates as detailed in table VIII.C.3. Sensitivity assumption: reduce the non-compliance rates by 50 percent (i.e., assume higher baseline compliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of uncertainty about current provision of rest breaks (union contracts, State laws, etc.), halving non-compliance rates decreased estimated annualized total costs by nearly $2.1 billion (approximately 27%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity test — adoption of OSHA HIIPP template
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary assumption: 90 percent of employers with >10 employees and all employers with ≤10 employees without an existing HIIPP will use OSHA template; Sensitivity assumption: 100% of all employers use OSHA template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming all employers use the template would lower estimated annualized costs by about $7.8 million (≈0.1%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity test — travel time to/from rest break area
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary assumption: travel time to rest breaks = 2 minutes for indoor and 4 minutes for outdoor employees. Sensitivity assumption: travel time = 3 minutes for indoor and 6 minutes for outdoor employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing travel time increased estimated annualized costs by approximately $1.4 billion (about 18.1%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity test — recovered break time through improved productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary assumption: ~70% of break time offset by increased productivity. Sensitivity assumption: 100% of break time offset by increased productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming 100% productivity recovery (i.e., full offset) reduces the cost of the proposed standard by about $2.5 billion; changing this assumption materially affects total cost estimates. OSHA notes literature limitations and alternative calculations (appendix A) that suggest offsets up to 100%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and adjustment for revenue estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Most revenue numbers used to determine cost-to-revenue ratios were obtained from the 2017 SUSB (Census Bureau) and adjusted to 2023 dollars using the BEA GDP deflator. For industries missing from SUSB, OSHA used alternative sources/methods (e.g., USDA Census of Agriculture for agriculture; Census Bureau state/local finance data for local governments; QCEW wage-to-receipts ratio approach for rail, postal, insurance funds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA considers SUSB 2017 the best available source; where unavailable, OSHA documents alternative sources and adjusts to 2023 dollars. Specific methods for deriving revenues for NAICS groups (e.g., aquaculture) and for government entities are described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of costs as variable vs fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: A large percentage of the costs of this proposed standard are variable because they depend primarily on the number and types of employees at an establishment; fixed costs exist but are less dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variable costs vary with output and employment; fixed costs (e.g., initial capital) can be more limiting because they are not easily adjusted. OSHA highlights implications for how industries absorb and pass on costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicating ability to absorb or pass on costs
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA examines factors such as whether all establishments in an industry are covered by the standard (reducing competitive disadvantage), presence of foreign competition not subject to the rule, availability of close substitute goods/services, and whether services must be performed domestically (reducing international competition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When all establishments in an affected industry are subject to the standard, competitors do not gain an economic advantage and substitution by an uncovered industry is less likely. Conversely, foreign competition or close substitutes can limit firms' ability to pass on costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further analysis when industries fail the screening test
rubrics_metrics.description: Industries that fail the revenue screening test (costs ≥1% of revenues) are not automatically deemed infeasible; they require additional examination to evaluate whether the standard would threaten the existence or competitive structure of those industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA will conduct more in-depth analysis for flagged industries consistent with case law (e.g., United Steelworkers v. Marshall, N. Am.'s Bldg. Trades Unions v. OSHA) rather than declaring infeasibility solely on the screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of published precedent and cross-agency practice to justify methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA explains methodological choices (e.g., reliance on revenue test) with reference to prior agency practice, judicial decisions, and other agencies' approaches (EPA, MSHA), using those precedents to support the chosen screening metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites case law and other agencies' practices to justify relying on revenue rather than profit measures, and discusses limitations of profit data and prior experience where profit screens were distracting or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and solicitation of public input on assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA welcomes input from the public regarding aspects of the sensitivity analysis, including any data or information regarding accuracy of preliminary estimates of compliance costs and benefits and how estimates may be affected by varying assumptions and methodological approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural statement signals that the analysis and key assumptions are open for public comment and that revisions may follow based on submitted evidence or arguments.
